title: Living ashtpadi 12
hookLine: humility is the doorway to every virtue in Sukhmani

cards: Two words, said badly or said well, can change a whole evening: I'm sorry. Most of us know exactly how hard they are. You rehearse them in the car.
You add a but. You explain why it wasn't really your fault before you reach the part where it was. The apology gets stuck somewhere between the throat and the pride.
And when someone finally says it plainly, no but, no speech, something in the room loosens. Sukhmani has spent a whole ashtpadi on why.

teach.b: Sukhmani is twenty-four ashtpadis long, and the twelfth lands near the middle. Before it, Guru Arjan has talked about remembering the Name, the company of the holy, the One who does everything.
Here he names what all of that depends on.

teach.h: WHILE I AM THE DOER, NO PEACE.
teach.b: In the second stanza, in paraphrase: as long as a person thinks, something gets done by me, there's no peace for them. As long as they think, I am the doer, they keep going round and round.
The I is the blockage; while it stands in the doorway, nothing else comes through. That's why many Sikhs call humility the doorway to the other virtues.
Guru Nanak had already said something like it in Asa di Var, a hymn sung in many gurdwaras every morning: sweetness and humility, Nanak, are the essence of all virtue and goodness.
Mithat neevee, in Punjabi. Sweetness, and lowness. Notice the pair.
Humility in Sikh teaching is never sour, never a grim, hunched-over feeling of being nothing. It's sweet: easy to be around, quick to laugh, quick to say sorry.
An apology is humility in its smallest size. It says: I was the doer of this, and it wasn't right. Owning the mistake is the opposite of pride, because pride's whole job is to defend the self.
So the twelfth ashtpadi lands somewhere very ordinary: a kitchen, a car, a group chat, wherever two people have rubbed each other the wrong way.
Humility first, and then everything else has room.

how: Sikhs reciting Sukhmani Sahib read the twelfth ashtpadi's warnings about the I that claims to be the doer, and in many gurdwaras Asa di Var, with its line on sweetness and humility, is sung each morning.

o: sweetness and humility, the heart of virtue
a sweet dish shared after Sikh prayers
quiet shyness in front of other people

p: a morning hymn sung in gurdwaras

s: in Sikh teaching, humility is meant to feel grim and sour
Guru Nanak pairs it with sweetness: mithat neevee.
the twelfth ashtpadi says peace can't come while I am the doer
the I in the doorway blocks everything else.
the twelfth ashtpadi is the last of Sukhmani
Sukhmani has twenty-four; the twelfth sits near the middle.

games.q: you snapped at a friend. you want to apologize. which version fits the twelfth ashtpadi?
o: I'm sorry, but you started it.
games.why: the plain one. the but defends the self, which is pride's job; owning it lets the I step out of the doorway.

practice: Let the past week drift by, a sharp word, a late reply, a promise that slipped, and without hunting for big guilt, look for one small thing where you were the doer and it wasn't right.
When you find it, say the words silently and plainly, with no but on the end: I'm sorry. Feel how short the sentence is.

wordCard.voice: Mithat neevee, sweetness and lowness. Humility as the doorway: while I am the doer blocks it, nothing else comes through.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: mithat neevee, sweetness and humility, from Guru Nanak's Asa di Var.

carryVoice: Your line: humility first. Sweet, and low, and quick to say sorry. That's day four hundred eighty-five, done.
